Valarie Gildon, and Samuel Gildon, wife and husband and the marital community composed thereof, Respondents, v. Simon Property Group , d/b/a Northgate Mall and “XYZ Corporations 1-5” and “John Doe and Jane Does No. 1-5”, and the marital communities composed thereof, Petitioners
Arturo Alejandre and Norma Alejandre, husband and wife, Respondents, v. Mary M. Bull, a single person, Petitioner
facts: Respondent Arturo Alejandre and his wife Norma purchased a home from respondent Mary Bull. After the Alejandres subsequently discovered that the home’s septic system was defective, they filed suit against Bull in the Superior Court for Walla Walla County, claiming fraudulent and negligent misrepresentation. The trial court granted summary judgment for Bull, ruling that the Alejandres’ claims are barred by the economic loss rule, which bars recovery for breaches of tort duties where a contractual relationship exists between the parties and the losses are economic losses. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed and remanded the case for trial, holding that the economic loss rule is inapplicable insofar as the contract between Bull and the Alejandres did not allocate risk for fraudulent or negligent misrepresentation. Bull appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Are the Alejandres’ claims barred by the economic loss rule despite the fact that their contract with Bull did not allocate risk for fraudulent or negligent misrepresentation?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the Alejandres’ negligent misrepresentation claim is barred by the economic loss rule insofar as the economic loss rule applies regardless of whether the specific risk of loss at issue was allocated in the parties’ contract. The Court also held that although the Alejandres’ claim of fraudulent misrepresentation is not barred by the economic loss rule, the Alejandres failed to present sufficient evidence of fraud given that they failed to exercise the diligence required in investigating the condition of the septic system.

title: Public Utility District No. 2 of Grant County, Washington, a municipal corporation, Respondent, v. North American Foreign Trade Zone Industries , a Washington limited liability company, PACIFIC Northwest Bank, a Washington banking corporation, Petitioners
facts: After failing to reach an agreement with petitioner North American Foreign Trade Zone Industries, L.L.C. to purchase land that it was leasing, the respondent Public Utility District #2 of Grant County decided to acquire the property by condemnation. The Public Utility District subsequently petitioned the Superior Court for Grant County to condemn the property. The superior court condemned the property, ruling that the Public Utility District had complied with the statutory notice requirements for the initiation of an eminent domain action and had established public use and necessity. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed. North American Foreign Trade Zone Industries appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the Public Utility District comply with the statutory notice requirements for the initiation of an eminent domain action? If so, did the Public Utility District establish public use and necessity?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the notice the Public Utility District provided to the public of the meeting of the Grant County Commission authorizing the condemnation of the property satisfied the notice requirements of Washington Revised Code §35.22.288, Washington Revised Code §35.23.221, Washington Revised Code §35.27.300, and Washington Revised Code §35.30.010. The Court also held that the Public Utility district established that the condemnation was for a public use as the purpose of the condemnation was to allow the Public Utility District to continue operating generators on the property in order to continue providing energy to its customers. Furthermore, the Court found that the condemnation was also necessary insofar as the decision to install the generators was motivated by the need for a backup facility in the event of an interruption in the supply of energy from other sources.

title: In re An, Attorney at Law
State v. Smith
facts: Petitioner Sarah Smith was convicted of second degree assault with a deadly weapon in the Superior Court for Pierce County after a trial in which the jury was instructed that a person commits second degree assault when under circumstances not amounting to first degree assault they assault another with a deadly weapon. The jury was also given additional instructions setting forth the three common law definitions of assault. Smith appealed her conviction, asserting that these definitions constituted alternative means of committing the crime and that her right to a unanimous jury verdict was violated when the state of Washington failed to present substantial evidence to support convicting her under each of these definitions. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Smith’s conviction. Smith appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the common law definitions of assault that were provided to the jury constitute alternative means of committing the crime?
conclusions: Chief Justice Alexander’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the common law definitions of assault that were provided to the jury were not alternative means of committing the crime as these definitions merely define the element of assault.

title: State v. Pillatos
facts: Respondent David Pillatos pled guilty to first degree murder in the Superior Court for Pierce County. Prior to sentencing, the United States Supreme Court decided in Blakely v. Washington that aggravating factors supporting an exceptional sentence must be proven to the jury beyond a reasonable doubt. Consequently, the state of Washington moved to empanel a sentencing jury. The trial court denied the motion, ruling that the procedures set forth in the new provisions of Washington Revised Code §9.94A, which was amended in response to Blakely, cannot be applied retroactively and that it lacks the inherent authority to empanel a sentencing jury. The state of Washington appealed this decision directly to the Supreme Court of Washington.
